content.text:
While the dimension lookups run, I'll work out the layout and build steps from what's already confirmed.

The board is 120 × 108 mm. J4 (comms) and J5 (relays) sit along one long edge; J7 (power/GPIO) and J11 (cable) sit along the other. The RJ45 jack is on the short right edge. Mounted with the 120 mm side along the rail, J4/J5 face up and J7/J11 face down toward the power rail, which keeps the signal wiring short.

Working out the wiring showed two things the current BOM handles badly:
1. **The 24 V supply tap.** It comes off L1/L2 at 18 AWG, and a UT 16 clamp shouldn't take an 8 AWG and an 18 AWG conductor together. The clean fix is a second UT 16 per leg, joined with a plug-in bridge.
2. **PE connection points.** PE needs four: cord ground, J1772 ground, PS1 earth and the 0 V bond. One UT 16-PE only has two clamps, so it needs a second PE terminal.

I asked the dimensions agent for the bridge part number. Once it reports back, I'll add these parts to the BOM.

I found sizes for all 12 parts, but a few gaps matter for the drawing:

- **Gaps:** I couldn't confirm which way the UM-PRO PCB sits relative to the rail, and I found no clearance-hole size for the Bimed glands.
- **Different numbers than you expected:** the EH04-11N contacts are 21-22 and 33-34 (not 13-14), the HDR-60 has no FG terminal, and the SDM230 terminal layout depends on the version.

Everything below is saved in `/tmp/opencode/dims/summary.md`.

W = width along the rail, H = height across the rail as seen from the front, D = depth. All values are in mm.

**Terminal layouts (as seen from the front)**
- **UT 16 / UT 16-PE:** one screw on the top edge and one on the bottom edge. Wire range is 1.5–25 mm² (AWG 16–4), 1–16 mm² with a ferrule; strip 14 mm.
- **ESB63-20N-01:** the catalog symbol shows **A1, 1, 3 on top** and **A2, 2, 4 on the bottom**.
  - The drawing is of the 4-pole housing: 4 main screws per edge, with a small coil screw between poles 2 and 3 on each edge.
  - I didn't find which screw positions the 2-pole version actually uses.
  - Main wires: 1.5–25 mm² rigid, 1.5–16 mm² flexible.
- **EH04-11N:** clips onto the **left side** of the contactor.
  - **Terminals are 21-22 (NC) and 33-34 (NO), not 13-14.** 21 and 33 are on top; 22 and 34 are on the bottom.
  - Each edge has two screws stacked across the rail. The drawing doesn't show which number is the outer one.
- **SDM230 (current V1.9 manual drawing):**
  - **Top edge:** 1 = L-in (left), 2 = L-out (right).
  - **Bottom edge:** a small terminal strip sits above the large terminals, left to right: 5 = A, 6 = B, 7 = GND, 8 = pulse 1 +, 9 = COM, 10 = pulse 2 +. Below it are the large terminals 3 = N-in (left) and 4 = N-out (right).
  - An older Eastron Europe manual also shows a "V2" layout: 1 L-in and 2 N-in on top, 3 L-out and 4 N-out on the bottom. **Check the label on your unit before drawing it.**
- **HDR-60-24:**
  - **Top edge**, left to right: 1 −V, 2 −V, 3 +V, 4 +V, then the voltage-adjust pot.
  - **Bottom edge**, at the left: 5 AC/L, 6 AC/N.
  - **There is no FG/PE terminal.**
- **FAZ-C2/2:** **1 and 3 on top, 2 and 4 on the bottom** (Eaton two-pole connection diagram in the AutomationDirect spec: https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/specs/eatonfaz.pdf). Wires 1×25 or 2×10 mm².
- **UM-PRO PCB orientation: not found.** The datasheet says only "Mounting position: parallel to the DIN rail". The product photo suggests the 120 mm side runs along the rail, but no source says so. Confirm with Phoenix's CAD drawing (their site blocked the bot).

**10. Panel devices**

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schneider XB5AA31 | Ø22.5 recommended (Ø22.3 +0.4) | 9 | 43, plus 23.6 per extra contact row | Body 30 × 41.5; centre spacing 40 × 30 |
| Schneider XB5AVB3 | Ø22.5 | 11 | 43 | Body 30 × 41.5 |
| AutomationDirect GCX3131 | Ø22.5 | not given | 45 with one contact layer, plus 26 per extra layer | Mushroom Ø40; depth is from the generic GCX plastic drawing, not a part-specific one |

Sources: https://www.se.com/us/en/product/download-pdf/XB5AA31, https://www.se.com/us/en/product/download-pdf/XB5AVB3, https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/specs/gcx22mmpb.pdf

**11. Polycase DR-62:** **one rail per kit**, 35 × 7.5 × **375 mm**, mounted "along the length" of the ZH-161407. (The DR-60 is a 325 mm rail that runs along its width.) This is from the search snippet only, because Polycase blocks the bot: https://www.polycase.com/dr-62

**12. Bimed glands** (AutomationDirect catalog and drawings)

| Part | Thread | Cable range | Hex size | Largest outer Ø | Height above wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BM-ENX-15-W | M40×1.5 | 19–28 | SW 46 (52.4 across corners) | 55.3 overall; lock nut 50.0 | 45.5 |
| BM-ENX-12-W | M20×1.5 | 6–12 | SW 24 (27.7 across corners) | 28.6 overall; lock nut 26.0 | 29.0 |

The thread length is 10 mm on both. **Clearance hole / drill size: not found.** Sources: https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/specs/bimedglands.pdf, https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/drawings/BM-ENX-15-W.pdf, https://cdn.automationdirect.com/static/drawings/BM-ENX-12-W.pdf

The measurements change the drawings and two wiring decisions:

- **The contactor is 54 mm wide** (3 modules), not 36 mm.
- **The Mean Well supply has no earth terminal**, so it only needs L and N.
- **The meter only needs N as a voltage reference**, so L2 doesn't have to pass through it. I'll feed that reference from the protected side of the 2 A breaker (FAZ terminals take two conductors). The J1772 cable then lands straight on the contactor output, which removes the second terminal group.
- **PE gets three PE terminals** next to the input terminals, for the cord ground, the J1772 ground and the 0 V bond.

I'm writing the generator now: real part outlines placed on the two 375 mm DR-62 rails inside the box's 397 × 346 mm interior, at 1 SVG unit per mm.

I've added an **Assembly** section after the build notes in `/home/brian/gl/cb-l2-evse.html`. It has 10 numbered steps, and the seven steps that install parts or route wires each have a to-scale drawing.

**The drawings**
- **Scale:** 1 unit = 1 mm, looking into the enclosure base (397 × 346 mm inside) with the cover open. Each has a 100 mm scale bar.
- **What's shown:** two 375 mm DR-62 rails, the three glands on the bottom wall, and S2 on the right wall.
- **Part outlines** use manufacturer dimensions, for example the contactor at 54 × 85 mm, the meter at 36 × 100, the 24 V supply at 52.5 × 90, the board housing at 123.8 × 127.8, and the 12.2 mm terminals. The board's connectors are placed from its own PCB file.
- **Each step** shows the new parts and wires in colour and earlier ones in grey. Wires are drawn to the actual screws, with 8 AWG drawn thicker than 18 AWG.

**The steps**
1. Prepare the enclosure: drill the gland holes and the S2 hole, and fit both rails.
2. Fit the lower (power) rail.
3. Fit the upper (control) rail.
4. Wire the power path in 8 AWG.
5. Wire the 24 V supply.
6. Wire the control signals.
7. Connect the PC and configure EVerest.
8. Check it with the power off.
9. Bring it up on the Pionix kit's 24 V supply only, with a J1772 EV simulator.
10. First run on 240 V.

**Design changes from laying it out**
- **The J1772 cable now lands directly on K1**, so the second terminal group (TB2) is gone. TT1 now sticks to the contactor body.
- **L2 no longer passes through the meter.** It only needs N as a voltage reference, so that lead now comes from the protected side of the 2 A breaker.
- **Each 24 V supply tap gets its own terminal.** TB1-1/TB1-2 and TB1-3/TB1-4 are joined with plug-in bridges, so an 18 AWG tap never shares a clamp with 8 AWG.
- **There are three PE terminals**: cord ground, J1772 ground and the 0 V bond.
- **The Mean Well supply has no earth terminal**, so I removed its ground from Sheet 1.

**BOM changes:** required parts are now **$873.47**, up from $865.09.
- +2 PE terminals
- 2 FBS 2-12 bridges ($2.66 each)
- 4 end clamps instead of 2
- About 1 m each of 18 AWG black, red and green, not priced

**Check before you drill or wire:**
- **Rail mounting:** confirm the enclosure base has mounting bosses for both rails. If it only has centred ones, use the ZX-1614K panel.
- **Board orientation:** Phoenix doesn't say which way the board sits in the UM-PRO housing. I drew the 120 mm side along the rail.
- **Screw positions:** the datasheets don't dimension the screws on the contactor, aux contact and meter. Those positions in the drawings are approximate; check the labels on your parts.
- **Hole sizes:** Bimed doesn't publish gland hole sizes, so I used the usual thread size plus 0.5 mm (40.5 and 20.5 mm).

The scripts that build the drawings and the BOM are `/tmp/opencode/build_assembly.py` and `/tmp/opencode/build_bom.py`. Move them out of `/tmp` if you want to keep them, and re-run them to regenerate both sections after any changes.

<skill_content name="OpenCode">
# Skill: OpenCode

# OpenCode

Use this guide as the starting point for work involving OpenCode itself. It
covers the core concepts needed to configure and customize OpenCode, extend it
with plugins, and build integrations with the OpenCode SDK, clients, and API.

Full documentation is available at <https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/>. This overview is
only an index of core concepts. Before answering a question about a topic below,
fetch the URL named in that section and use the full page as the source of
truth. Follow links from that page when the question needs more detail. Fetch
<https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/> first when you need to discover the relevant
documentation page.

A machine-readable documentation index is available at
<https://opencode.ai/v2/llms.txt>.

## Version policy

Always answer for OpenCode V2 unless the user explicitly asks about V1,
legacy OpenCode, or migrating from V1.

Use only <https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/> documentation as the source of truth for V2.
Do not use <https://opencode.ai/docs/>, which documents V1, and do not use
general web search to resolve a V2 documentation question when the V2 docs or
linked pages cover it. The schema served from
<https://opencode.ai/config.json> accepts both V2 fields and deprecated V1
fields. Never recommend a field it marks deprecated. If V2 documentation is
missing or contradictory, state the uncertainty or ask for clarification instead of falling back to V1.

V1 documentation and syntax may be consulted only when the user explicitly
asks about V1 or when needed as migration input. Outputs and recommendations
must still use V2 unless the user specifically requests a V1 result.

## [CLI](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli)

For questions about the terminal interface, command-line invocation, `run`,
`mini`, terminal providers, or other CLI behavior, fetch the
[CLI guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli) and the relevant page linked from
that section.

CLI and TUI preferences are separate from OpenCode's server and project
configuration. They live in the global `~/.config/opencode/cli.json`, or
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/cli.json` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set. There is no
project-local CLI configuration. Set `OPENCODE_CLI_CONFIG_CONTENT` to merge
inline JSON over the global settings. Most preferences can also be changed from
the TUI by pressing `Ctrl+P` and selecting **Open settings**.

### [Settings](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config)

Fetch the full [CLI settings reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config)
before editing `cli.json`. It documents every terminal-only setting, accepted
values, and examples, including themes, input, sessions, tabs, diffs, alerts,
Mini, keybindings, terminal plugins, and debugging. Do not put these settings
in `opencode.json(c)`.

### [Keybinds](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/keybinds)

Configure keybindings under `keybinds` in `cli.json`. The leader key is the
`keybinds.leader` entry; leader timing is configured separately under
`leader.timeout`. Bindings can use a string, an array of strings, or an object
when event behavior such as `preventDefault` is required. Disable a binding
with `"none"` or `false`.

Never guess a command ID, default binding, or accepted key syntax. Fetch the
full [keybind reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/keybinds), which lists
the current IDs and defaults, before answering or editing a binding.

## [OpenCode configuration](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config)

OpenCode's server and project configuration uses JSON or JSONC. Include the
published schema so the user's editor can validate fields and provide
autocomplete:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
}
```

Global configuration lives at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json(c)` and applies
to every project for that user. Project configuration can live in any directory
as `opencode.json(c)` or `.opencode/opencode.json(c)`, including nested packages
in a monorepo.

During ordinary project discovery, OpenCode searches the current Location
directory and every ancestor through the filesystem root, including directories
above the detected project or repository root. It merges direct
`opencode.json(c)` files from the farthest ancestor to the current directory,
then does the same for `.opencode/opencode.json(c)` files. This means every
discovered `.opencode` config overrides every discovered direct config. Global
filesystem configuration has lower precedence than these discovered documents.

Common configuration fields include `model`, `default_agent`, `permissions`,
`agents`, `commands`, `plugins`, `providers`, `mcp`, `skills`, `instructions`,
`references`, `formatter`, and `lsp`.

This configuration is distinct from `cli.json`. Use the
[CLI settings reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config) for terminal
preferences, especially themes and keybindings.

Config changes apply without a restart. OpenCode watches config files and
reloads agents, commands, skills, MCP servers, and plugins after a save. The TUI
does the same for `cli.json`. To force a full reload, use `/reload`. Don't tell
the user to restart OpenCode after editing config.

Do not guess field names or shapes. Fetch the V2 configuration guide and its
linked topic guide as the source of truth, and preserve unrelated settings when
editing an existing file. Keep the published `$schema` URL in configuration
examples, but do not fetch it to determine the V2 configuration shape.

See the [full configuration guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config) for
every field, examples, config locations, and links to dedicated feature guides.

## [MCP servers](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers)

Configure MCP servers under `mcp.servers`. Prefer the CLI because it preserves
unrelated configuration. Use `--global` when the user asks to set up a service
for themselves without limiting it to the current project; omit it when they
explicitly want project-local configuration.

```sh
opencode mcp add <name> --global --url <remote-url>
opencode mcp list
```

Remote servers use OAuth by default. If `mcp list` reports that a server needs
authentication, tell the user to run `/mcps`, select the server, and sign in.
Do not run `opencode mcp auth` through the shell tool: it starts an interactive
flow whose authorization link can be hidden in background process output.
Use the user-facing MCP interface instead.

Report the server as configured but awaiting sign-in until its connection
status confirms it is connected.

OAuth credentials are stored outside the OpenCode configuration. Do not ask for or
store an API key when the server supports OAuth. Use header-based credentials
only when OAuth is unavailable or the user explicitly requires them, and use an
environment substitution such as `{env:MCP_API_KEY}` instead of writing a
secret into configuration.

## [V1 to V2 migration](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1)

For any request to migrate OpenCode configuration, agents, commands, skills,
plugins, integrations, or other behavior from V1 to V2, read the full
[migration guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1) before acting. In
the repository, its source is `services/www/src/docs/content/migrate-v1.mdx`.

V1 config files and `.opencode/` definitions are intended to remain compatible.
The only intentional breaking changes are the server API and plugin API. Native
V2 config uses more ergonomic shapes, but conversion is optional. When the user
requests conversion, inspect the complete configuration, preserve behavior and
unrelated settings, and apply only the relevant migrations from the guide. For
plugin migrations, fetch and follow both the migration guide and the full
[plugins guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins). If non-API V1
functionality fails in V2, use the `report` skill to file it as a compatibility
bug.

## [Plugins](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins)

For questions about creating, configuring, loading, publishing, or migrating
plugins, fetch the full [plugins guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins)
before answering. Refer to this guide when the user wants to build a plugin. It
covers hooks, transforms, tools, plugin context capabilities, and package
entrypoints. Plugins can also extend the TUI; for those, fetch the
[CLI plugin guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/cli).
For custom methods and events shared with other plugins or clients, fetch the
[RPC guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/rpc).

## [Service](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting#check-the-background-service)

OpenCode uses a client-server architecture. Interfaces such as the TUI connect
to a background OpenCode service, which owns sessions, configuration, plugins,
permissions, and tool execution.

OpenCode normally discovers or starts the shared background service
automatically. Restart it only if it is stuck or unhealthy, not to apply
configuration changes:

```sh
opencode service restart
```

Check its status after restarting:

```sh
opencode service status
```

## [API](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/api)

OpenCode exposes an HTTP API from its server. The API is described by an
OpenAPI document available from the running server at `/openapi.json`.

Use OpenCode's built-in `api` command for local requests. It uses the same
discovery and authentication flow as the TUI and may start the background
service when no compatible healthy service is available. It accepts either an
HTTP method and path or an OpenAPI operation ID.

Call an endpoint with an HTTP method and path:

```sh
opencode api get /api/info
```

Pass a request body with `--data` or `-d`, and additional headers with
`--header` or `-H`:

```sh
opencode api post /api/example --data '{"key":"value"}'
opencode api get /api/example --header 'X-Example:value'
```

Request bodies default to `Content-Type: application/json`. When OpenCode is
connected to an explicit server instead of its managed background service, use
the same configured server and authentication context rather than constructing
an unauthenticated request separately.

See the [full API reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/api) for available
endpoints, parameters, request bodies, and response schemas. The
raw [OpenAPI specification](https://opencode.ai/v2/openapi.json) is also
available for code generation and other tooling.

## [Client](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/client)

For questions about connecting an application to OpenCode over the network,
fetch the full [client guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/client) before
answering.

`@opencode/client` is the generated TypeScript client for the OpenCode HTTP
API. Its methods and types come from the same contract as the API reference.
The default entrypoint exposes Promise-based resource clients and async
iterables for streaming endpoints. The `@opencode/client/effect` entrypoint
exposes typed Effects, Streams, and decoded OpenCode schema values. Its
`Service` API can discover, start, stop, and authenticate with the local
background service from a Node application.

## [SDK](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk)

For questions about embedding OpenCode directly in an application, fetch the
full [SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk) before answering. The SDK
hosts OpenCode in the application without opening an HTTP listener.

Use the [Effect SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk/effect) for
Effect applications. For Cloudflare Durable Objects, use the
[Cloudflare SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk/cloudflare).

## [Troubleshooting](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting)

OpenCode runs a client and a background server. Start by determining whether a
problem belongs to the client, the shared server, or one project.

- Check the service with `opencode service status` and verify the API with
  `opencode api get /api/info`.
- Compare with `opencode --standalone`, which runs the TUI with a private
  server, to isolate shared-service issues.
- Inspect `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`. Filter `role=cli` for
  client startup and `role=server` for sessions, providers, plugins,
  permissions, and tools.
- Run one reproduction with `OPENCODE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` when normal logs are not
  sufficient.
- Do not delete or edit the database, service registration, or service config
  while diagnosing a problem. Back up persistent data before inspecting it
  with external tools.
- Redact API keys, authorization headers, prompts, file contents, and other
  sensitive data before sharing diagnostics.

See the [full troubleshooting guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting)
for service lifecycle commands, API inspection, log locations, explicit server
connections, issue-reporting details, and local development paths.

# Intro

Run the CLI in a project to open the full-screen terminal interface:

```bash
opencode
```

Pass a directory to work in a different project:

```bash
opencode ~/code/my-project
```

Suggested terminals:

- [Ghostty](https://ghostty.org)
- [WezTerm](https://wezterm.org)
- [Alacritty](https://alacritty.org)
- [Kitty](https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/)

Truecolor support gives themes their most accurate colors; terminals without it use an approximation of the available
palette.

## Automation

Use `opencode run` to submit a prompt without opening the interactive interface. It is designed for scripts, CI jobs, and
other workflows that need model output directly in the terminal.

```bash
opencode run "Explain this repository"
```

## Mini

Use `opencode mini` to start OpenCode's minimal interactive interface instead of the full-screen TUI.

```bash
opencode mini
```

Run `opencode mini --help` to see its session, model, agent, prompt, and replay options.

## Background service

By default, OpenCode discovers or starts one shared background server for your user account. Every local OpenCode client
connects to that server, which owns sessions, configuration, integrations, permissions, and tool execution.

Use `--standalone` to run with a private server, or `--server` to connect to a specific server URL:

```bash
opencode --standalone
opencode --server http://localhost:4096
```

To make private servers the default for CLI commands instead of starting the shared service, disable it:

```bash
opencode service set disabled true
opencode
```

This stops the running background service. `--server` still connects to an explicitly selected server; `opencode service start`
can still start the shared service explicitly. To return to automatic service use, run `opencode service unset disabled`.
Pairing requires the shared service and is unavailable while it is disabled.

See [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting) for shared service diagnostics and the [API reference](/api) for server endpoints.

## Paths

Print a specific local path for use with other tools:

```bash
opencode debug paths db
sqlite3 "$(opencode debug paths db)"
```

The optional selector accepts `db`, `home`, `data`, `config`, `cache`, `state`, `tmp`, `bin`, `log`, or `repos` and prints
only the path and a newline. The database path respects the release channel and `OPENCODE_DB`; relative database overrides
resolve under the data directory, and `:memory:` is printed as-is. This command does not start a server or open the database.

Omit the selector to show all paths with labels:

```bash
opencode debug paths
```

## Uninstall

Preview the files and installation that will be removed:

```bash
opencode uninstall --dry-run
```

Run `opencode uninstall` to confirm removal. OpenCode stops registered background services and persistent terminals before
removing the global cache directory, which is shared by OpenCode versions and channels. Session data, configuration, and
state are never removed.

- `--force` (`-f`) skips confirmation; use it for noninteractive removal.
- Package-manager installations use the detected package manager. Curl installations print the final command to remove
  the executable manually.

DESCRIPTION
  OpenCode command line interface

USAGE
  opencode <subcommand> [flags] [<directory>]

ARGUMENTS
  directory string    Directory to start OpenCode in (optional)

FLAGS
  --standalone            Run with a private server instead of the background service
  --server string         Connect to a server URL instead of the background service
  --auto                  Auto-approve permissions that are not explicitly denied
  --continue, -c          Continue the last session
  --session, -s string    Session ID to continue, or to create if it does not exist
  --prompt string         Prompt to use

GLOBAL FLAGS
  --help, -h                                                          Show help information
  --version, -v                                                       Show version information
  --wizard                                                            Start wizard mode for a command
  --completions <bash|zsh|fish|sh>                                    Print shell completion script (choices: bash, zsh, fish, sh)
  --log-level <all|trace|debug|info|warn|warning|error|fatal|none>    Sets the minimum log level (choices: all, trace, debug, info, warn, warning, error, fatal, none)
  --print-logs                                                        Print logs to stderr (server logs require --standalone)

SUBCOMMANDS
  upgrade, update    Upgrade OpenCode to the latest or a specific version
  uninstall          Uninstall OpenCode, keeping session data, configuration, and state
  acp                Start an Agent Client Protocol server
  api                Make a request to the running server
  debug              Debugging and troubleshooting tools
  auth               manage integrations and credentials
  mcp                Manage MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers
  plugin             Manage plugins
  models             List all available models
  stats              Show shareable usage statistics
  mini               Start the minimal interactive interface
  run                Run OpenCode with a message
  session            Manage sessions
  service            Manage the background server
  reload             Reload configuration
  pair               Print one-time links to connect a browser or app
  serve              Start the v2 API and web server
DESCRIPTION
  Manage sessions

USAGE
  opencode session <subcommand> [flags]

  --help, -h                                                          Show help information

  --completions <bash|zsh|fish|sh>                                    Print shell completion script (choices: bash, zsh, fish, sh)

  --print-logs                                                        Print logs to stderr (server logs require --standalone)

SUBCOMMANDS
  list      List top-level sessions in the current project, newest first
  delete    Delete a session and its child sessions
  export    Export session data as JSON
  import    Import session data from a JSON file or URL

# Instructions

Add an `AGENTS.md` file to give OpenCode persistent project guidance. Use it for build commands, architecture notes, code conventions, and verification requirements.

```md title="AGENTS.md"
# Project instructions

- Run `bun typecheck` after changing TypeScript.
- Keep database queries in `src/database`.
- Do not edit generated files directly.
```

Commit project instruction files so everyone working in the repository receives the same guidance.

## Scope

Place `AGENTS.md` in the directory where its guidance should apply. OpenCode loads the global file followed by every `AGENTS.md` from the current workspace directory toward the home directory. For workspaces outside the home directory, it stops at the project root.

```text
~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md
~/code/my-project/AGENTS.md
~/code/my-project/packages/AGENTS.md
~/code/my-project/packages/web/AGENTS.md  ← current workspace
```

In this example, all four files are loaded. They are combined in this order:

```text
~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md
packages/web/AGENTS.md
packages/AGENTS.md
AGENTS.md
```

Keep guidance that applies everywhere in the global file. Put repository-wide guidance at the project root and more specific guidance closer to the code it covers. OpenCode combines the files and does not resolve conflicts between them.

If the workspace is outside the project root, only the global file is loaded. Set `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1` to skip project `AGENTS.md` discovery without disabling the global file.

<Callout type="note">
  OpenCode V2 recognizes `AGENTS.md` only. It does not use `CLAUDE.md` as a fallback.
</Callout>

## Discovery

Instruction files below the workspace are discovered as the agent explores the project. Reading a file or listing a directory loads any `AGENTS.md` files between that target and the workspace.

```text
my-project/                         ← current workspace
├── AGENTS.md                       loaded initially
└── packages/
    └── web/
        ├── AGENTS.md               loaded when this area is read
        └── src/
            └── app.ts              read target
```

Nested files are loaded nearest-first and deduplicated while their instruction entry remains in model-visible history. Reading the same area again does not normally inject them again. If compaction or a revert removes that entry, a later read can load the file again.

Edits to a nested file are not detected automatically after it loads. Start a new session when updated text must apply immediately.

## Ordering

The selected agent or provider system prompt is sent first. OpenCode then assembles initial instructions in this order:

```text
1. Agent or provider system prompt
2. Code Mode tool guidance, when enabled
3. MCP server, reference, and skill guidance
4. Global and project AGENTS.md files, then configured instructions
5. Built-in date and environment context
6. Session-specific instruction entries supplied through the API
```

These sources are combined rather than used as overrides. Nested `AGENTS.md` files discovered later are added to session history in discovery order.

## Updates

Edit a global or upward-discovered `AGENTS.md` while a session is running to update its guidance.

```bash
$ printf '\n- Run the integration suite before committing.\n' >> AGENTS.md
```

Before the next model request, OpenCode detects the change and adds an instruction update before delivering pending input:

```text
AGENTS.md changes
→ instruction update
→ next prompt
```

- Removing every ambient `AGENTS.md` tells the session that the previous ambient instructions no longer apply.
- A temporary read failure preserves the last known instructions instead of treating them as deleted.
- Moving a session retains its instruction state, so guidance at the destination is introduced as an update.
- Committing a session revert clears its instruction state and reloads instructions before the next prompt.

Instruction values remain privileged. Clients can see which sources changed, but not their contents.

## Configuration

Use the `instructions` array to add files, glob patterns, or HTTP(S) URLs alongside discovered `AGENTS.md` files:

```jsonc title="opencode.jsonc"
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "instructions": [
    "CONTRIBUTING.md",
    "docs/guidelines/*.md",
    "~/rules/opencode.md",
    "https://example.com/instructions.md",
  ],
}
```

Configured instructions load after `AGENTS.md` files, in the order they are listed. Entries from every config document are combined.

| Entry                   | Resolution                                                           |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Relative path or glob   | Searched in each directory from the workspace up to the project root |
| `~/` path               | Resolved from your home directory                                    |
| Absolute path           | Used as written; the file name may be a glob                         |
| `http://` or `https://` | Fetched when config loads, with a five-second timeout                |

- Local files update like `AGENTS.md` when they change. New files matching a glob load on the next config change.
- Missing files are skipped. A URL that cannot be fetched is skipped, or keeps its last fetched content.
- With `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`, or when the workspace is outside the project, relative entries resolve against the global config directory.

# Project instructions

This repository is the design for a 9.6 kW (240 V / 40 A) Level 2 J1772 EV charger bench unit, built around the Pionix ChargeBridge evaluation board (CB-EVAL v1.2 with a CB-CCS-EVSE-LU module) and EVerest on an x86 PC. It's a private bench test device, not a listed product.

- `cb-l2-evse.html`: the deliverable. Schematic sheets 1–2, priced BOM, build notes, step-by-step assembly with to-scale drawings.
- `cb-eval-board/`: git submodule, Pionix's KiCad project. Its v1.2 schematic is authoritative over the v1.1 PDF datasheet (the PDF's J11 pin table is wrong).
- `datasheets/`: manufacturer PDFs (Git LFS), indexed in `datasheets/README.md`.
- `scripts/`: generators and tools; see `scripts/README.md`.
- `session/`: exported OpenCode session with the full design history.

## Working rules

- The BOM table and the Assembly section are generated. Edit `scripts/build_bom.py` or `scripts/build_assembly.py` and re-run them; don't hand-edit those parts of the HTML. Schematic sheets 1–2 and the build notes are hand-maintained SVG/HTML.
- Keep the schematic, BOM and assembly drawings consistent with each other. A wiring change usually touches all three.
- Never invent prices or dimensions. Record only values read from a vendor page or datasheet, with the date for prices, and mark anything unverified.
- Use `scripts/cfx search` / `scripts/cfx fetch` for web lookups (run `scripts/setup.sh` first). Polycase, Mouser and Home Depot block automated browsers; ask the user to save pages by hand.
- After editing the HTML, render it (for example `chromium --headless --screenshot`) and look at the result before reporting done.

## Design decisions to preserve

- Input: owned NEMA 14-50 cord on an existing 50 A GFCI circuit. N lands on isolated terminal TB1-5 and is never bonded to PE.
- CB-EVAL J11 has no ground pin. CP returns through the single 0 V–PE bond (PS1 −V to PE3).
- EMG IN (J4.11) has a 100 kΩ pull-up to 24 V. Any NC safety contact needs the R1/R2 2.2 kΩ divider to pull it low. The E-stop is optional; without it, leave J4.11 open.
- Relay 1 (J5.10 / J5.9) drives K1 through a TPS27S100, limited to about 5.2 A. Keep the coil under 2 A continuous and relay PWM off. K1 aux NC 21-22 goes from +24 V to J5.12, with R3 3.3 kΩ to 0 V for wetting current.
- The meter's N reference comes from F1/F2 terminal 4. L2 doesn't pass through the meter.

`session/cb-l2-evse.opencode-session.json` is the exported design session. In it, `/home/brian/gl` is this repository's root and `~/.local/bin/cfx` is now `scripts/cfx`.

# 9.6 kW Level 2 EV charger on the Pionix ChargeBridge eval board

Design files for a 240 V / 40 A, J1772 tethered, plug-in (NEMA 14-50) EVSE bench unit. A Pionix CB-EVAL v1.2 board with a ChargeBridge EVSE module handles the pilot and safety state machine, and EVerest runs on an external PC.

Open **`cb-l2-evse.html`** in a browser. It contains:

- Two schematic sheets: the power path, and control wiring with board connector pin numbers
- A BOM with vendor links and prices (read 26–27 Oct 2026, US shipping)
- Build notes, plus a 10-step assembly guide with to-scale layout and wiring drawings

> This is a bench test device for private use by someone qualified to work on 240 V equipment. It is not a listed product.

## Get it

Install [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com) first (`git lfs install`), then clone with the submodule:

```sh
git clone --recurse-submodules <this-repo-url> cb-l2-evse
cd cb-l2-evse
```

If you already cloned without it:

```sh
git submodule update --init
git lfs pull
```

## Contents

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `cb-l2-evse.html` | The design document |
| `cb-eval-board/` | Pionix CB-EVAL KiCad project (submodule, tag 1.2). Open with KiCad 9.0.3+ |
| `datasheets/` | Manufacturer datasheets for every major part (Git LFS); see `datasheets/README.md` |
| `scripts/` | BOM and assembly generators, KiCad netlister, web lookup tool; see `scripts/README.md` |
| `session/` | The OpenCode session the design was developed in |
| `AGENTS.md` | Project instructions that OpenCode loads automatically |

## Regenerate the document

The build scripts need only Python 3.10+:

```sh
python3 scripts/build_bom.py        # BOM table
python3 scripts/build_assembly.py   # assembly steps and drawings
```

For web lookups (price and datasheet research), set up the Camoufox tool once (about 600 MB):

```sh
scripts/setup.sh
scripts/cfx search "Mean Well HDR-60-24"
```

## Continue the design session in OpenCode

The full design conversation, including every tool call and the reasoning behind each decision, is in `session/cb-l2-evse.opencode-session.json`. To import it with this clone as its working directory:

```sh
opencode session import session/cb-l2-evse.opencode-session.json --directory "$(pwd)"
opencode session list          # find the imported session's ID
opencode -s <session-id>       # open it and keep going
```

The transcript refers to the original machine's paths: `/home/brian/gl` is the repository root, and `~/.local/bin/cfx` is `scripts/cfx`. `AGENTS.md` tells the agent this. Some tools used in the session (an MCP-driven Firefox sandbox, the original subagents) aren't part of this repo. The agent doesn't need them to pick up the work.

## Licensing

The `cb-eval-board` submodule is Pionix's, under CERN-OHL-P-2.0. Each datasheet belongs to its manufacturer and is included for reference.

- EMG IN (J4.11) has a 100 kΩ pull-up to 24 V. Any NC safety contact needs the R1/R2 2.2 kΩ divider to pull it low. The E-stop is optional; without it, leave J4.11 open.
- Relay 1 (J5.10 / J5.9) drives K1 through a TPS27S100, limited to about 5.2 A. Keep the coil under 2 A continuous and relay PWM off. K1 aux NC 21-22 goes from +24 V to J5.12, with R3 3.3 kΩ to 0 V for wetting current.
- The meter's N reference comes from F1/F2 terminal 4. L2 doesn't pass through the meter.

That's a Fedora/dnf5 syntax change rather than anything you did wrong. Fedora 41 and later ship dnf5, and in dnf5 `config-manager` takes subcommands instead of `--add-repo`. The first command did nothing because the plugin was already installed.

The simplest option is Fedora's own `gh` package, which needs no extra repo:

```sh
sudo dnf install gh
```

If you'd rather have GitHub's repo, which usually gets new releases sooner, use the dnf5 form:

```sh
sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --from-repofile=https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo dnf install gh --repo gh-cli
```

Then sign in:

```sh
gh auth login
```

Choose GitHub.com, HTTPS, and "Login with a web browser". When it asks, say yes to authenticating Git with your GitHub credentials, since that's what lets `git push` upload the LFS files. Run the login yourself rather than through me, because it's interactive and shows a one-time code.

Once `gh auth status` shows you're signed in, tell me. I'll then:
1. Create the public repo `briancappello/cb-l2-evse`.
2. Replace `<this-repo-url>` in the README with the real URL and commit.
3. Re-export the session so it includes this last stretch, and commit.
4. Push the commits and the 48 LFS files (about 40 MB, well within GitHub's free LFS limits).

Making it public also publishes the manufacturer PDFs and your email in the session export, as I mentioned earlier. If you'd rather keep the PDFs out, I can swap them for a download script before pushing.

# Publish cb-l2-evse.html to GitHub Pages as the site's index page.
name: Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [master]
    paths: [cb-l2-evse.html, .github/workflows/pages.yml]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v6
      - name: Assemble site
        run: |
          mkdir -p _site
          cp cb-l2-evse.html _site/index.html
          cp cb-l2-evse.html _site/cb-l2-evse.html
          touch _site/.nojekyll
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

Simulation splits into three layers here, and the best tool differs for each. Everything recommended below runs natively on your machine. All three packages are in Fedora's aarch64 repos and none are installed yet: **ngspice 47**, **KiCad 10.0.7** and **Qucs-S 25.2**.

## 1. Analog circuits: SPICE

These are the circuits in our design that are worth simulating:

| Circuit | What a simulation shows |
|---|---|
| EMG IN loop: R1/R2, the board's 100 kΩ pull-up, the 20 kΩ / 1 MΩ / 5.1 V zener input, the Schmitt buffer | Run ≈ 12 V and trip ≈ 0.5 V across resistor tolerance and a 21.6–29 V supply. Current into SW2 when it shorts the loop. |
| K1 feedback with R3 | Wetting current through the aux contact (target above 5 mA). Logic levels at J5.12. |
| Control pilot: ±12 V 1 kHz PWM, 1 kΩ source, cable capacitance, EV states B/C/D (2.74 kΩ / 1.3 kΩ / diode) | 9 / 6 / 3 V plateaus and edge rise times at the 1600 pF limit. This also checks the EV simulator rig you'll use in step 9. |
| PT1000 bridge + INA333 | Temperature-to-ADC curve, and error from resistor tolerance (Monte Carlo). |
| TPS27S100 driving the K1 coil | Inrush against the 5.2 A limit, and the turn-off clamp. TI publishes a PSpice model (SLVMC96A). It may not run in ngspice, and the ESB63's electronic coil isn't a simple inductor, so this one is only approximate. |

The ChargeBridge module is proprietary, so its pilot generator would be modelled from the J1772 reference circuit rather than Pionix's actual design.

**Tools:**
- **ngspice (recommended).** Open source, scriptable, and the simulator built into KiCad.
  - **Install:** `sudo dnf install ngspice`.
  - **Scripting:** the actively maintained Python wrapper is **spicelib** (1.6.4, Oct 2026), which also drives Xyce and LTspice. PySpice hasn't had a release since 2021.
  - **What it would give the repo:** simulations under `scripts/sim/`, run by GitHub Actions on every push, with result plots added to the Pages document.
- **KiCad 10's built-in simulator.** Opens the Pionix project, which is in KiCad 9 format. You could probe the board's real level-shifter and PT1000 circuits straight from the schematic once SPICE models are attached.
- **Qucs-S.** A GUI front end for ngspice, if you'd rather draw schematics than write netlists.
- **Falstad CircuitJS.** Runs in a browser, so nothing to install. Good for animated demos of the pilot states or the E-stop loop, and those could be embedded on the GitHub Pages site.
- **LTspice, TINA-TI, PSpice for TI.** Windows-only. On Asahi they'd need Wine with FEX x86 emulation, which Asahi users report as unreliable. Not worth it here.

## 2. Charging behaviour: EVerest software-in-the-loop

The state machine, current limits, metering, OCPP and stop handling are software, so SPICE doesn't apply to them. EVerest ships simulation modules in `modules/Simulation`:
- **YetiSimulator** stands in for the charger hardware and generates control pilot states.
- **SlacSimulator** covers the PLC handshake.
- **TemperatureSensorSimulator**, **IMDSimulator** and **OVMSimulator** fake the sensors.
- **EvseManagerSimulator** is a newer addition.

Paired with EVerest's simulated car, this runs a complete charging session on your x86 PC with no hardware. You could build the EVerest config there (40 A limit, SDM230, PT1000 limits) before the board is even wired.

## 3. Hardware-in-the-loop with real parts

Pionix sells the **car-side** ChargeBridge kit (€950 in yesterday's price lookup). The same board with an EV module acts as a real car on your bench, plugged into the J1772 handle, and it can run ISO 15118. It's the most realistic test short of an actual car, and it would replace the resistor-and-diode simulator in step 9.

## Recommendation

Start with ngspice plus spicelib: it takes one `dnf install`, runs natively, and can live in the repo and run on every push. I'd simulate the E-stop loop, feedback wetting, pilot states and PT1000 first, because those circuits carry assumptions we haven't checked. Run EVerest SIL on the PC in parallel. Buy the car-side kit only if you want more realism.

Should I set up the ngspice simulations? You'd need to run `sudo dnf install ngspice` (and `kicad` if you want the GUI); I'd write the netlists and add them to the repo and the published page.

#!/usr/bin/env python3 """Circuit simulations for the cb-l2-evse design (ngspice). python3 scripts/sim/run.py run everything, write netlists, update cb-l2-evse.html python3 scripts/sim/run.py --check run everything and exit non-zero if any check fails Component values come from the CB-EVAL v1.2 KiCad netlist (kicad-cli) and from the design's BOM. Thresholds for the board's 74LVC1G17 Schmitt inputs come from TI's datasheet (datasheets/TI_SN74LVC1G17_schmitt_buffer.pdf), interpolated to 3.3 V. """ import argparse, html, itertools, math, re, shutil, subprocess, sys, tempfile from pathlib import Path ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] NETDIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "netlists" NGSPICE = shutil.which("ngspice") VT_HI = 2.08 # 74LVC1G17 VT+ max at 3.3 V: input is guaranteed to read high above this VT_LO = 1.01 # 74LVC1G17 VT- min at 3.3 V: input is guaranteed to read low below this SUPPLY = (21.6, 24.0, 29.0) # HDR-60-24 adjustment range and nominal CLOSED, OPEN = 0.05, 1e12 # contact resistance models (ohms) ZENER = ".model DZ D(IS=1e-14 N=1 RS=20 BV=5.1 IBV=1m)" # MM3Z5V1 (only its clamp matters) D1N4148 = ".model D1N4148 D(IS=2.52n RS=0.568 N=1.752 BV=100 IBV=100u CJO=4p TT=20n)" CHECKS = [] # (group, description, value_text, passed) def check(group, desc, value, ok): CHECKS.append((group, desc, value, bool(ok))) def ngspice(name, deck): NETDIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) (NETDIR / f"{name}.cir").write_text(deck) with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td: path = Path(td) / "deck.cir" path.write_text(deck.replace("@WRDIR@", td)) r = subprocess.run([NGSPICE, "-b", str(path)], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300) out = r.stdout + r.stderr data = {} for f in Path(td).glob("*.dat"): data[f.stem] = [tuple(float(x) for x in ln.split()) for ln in f.read_text().split("\n") if ln.strip()] if r.returncode != 0 or "error" in out.lower() and "no error" not in out.lower(): bad = [ln for ln in out.splitlines() if "rror" in ln] if bad: raise RuntimeError(f"ngspice failed on {name}:\n" + "\n".join(bad[:10])) vals = {} for m in re.finditer(r"^\s*([\w().:+-]+)\s*=\s*([-+0-9.eE]+)\s*$", out, re.M): vals[m.group(1).lower()] = float(m.group(2)) return vals, data def tol_corners(nominals, tol): keys = list(nominals) for signs in itertools.product((-1, 1), repeat=len(keys)): yield {k: nominals[k] * (1 + s * tol) for k, s in zip(keys, signs)} # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1. Emergency input loop (J4.11): board R9/R43/R76/D22, our R1/R2 and NC contact chain # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- def emg_deck(vs, r, chain, sw2, r2_present=True): return f"""* EMG IN loop, J4.11 (CB-EVAL LevelShiftInput2 + R1/R2) V24 vp 0 {vs} Rchain vp a {chain} R1 a emg {r['R1']} R2 emg 0 {r['R2'] if r2_present else OPEN} R9 vp emg {r['R9']} R43 emg x {r['R43']} R76 x 0 {r['R76']} D22 0 x DZ Rsw2 emg 0 {sw2} {ZENER} .control op print v(emg) v(x) v(a) .endc .end """ def sim_emg(): nom = {"R1": 2200, "R2": 2200, "R9": 100e3, "R43": 20e3, "R76": 1e6} rows = [] worst = {"run": (1e9, None), "trip": (-1e9, None)} for vs in SUPPLY: for r in tol_corners(nom, 0.01): for state, chain in (("run", CLOSED), ("trip", OPEN)): v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(vs, r, chain, OPEN)) x = v["v(x)"] if state == "run" and x < worst["run"][0]: worst["run"] = (x, (vs, v["v(emg)"])) if state == "trip" and x > worst["trip"][0]: worst["trip"] = (x, (vs, v["v(emg)"])) v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(24, nom, CLOSED, OPEN)) rows.append(("NC chain closed (normal)", v["v(emg)"], v["v(x)"], "high")) v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(24, nom, OPEN, OPEN)) rows.append(("NC chain open or wire broken", v["v(emg)"], v["v(x)"], "low")) v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(24, nom, CLOSED, CLOSED)) i_sw2 = (24 - v["v(emg)"]) / nom["R1"] + (24 - v["v(emg)"]) / nom["R9"] rows.append(("On-board SW2 pressed, chain closed", v["v(emg)"], v["v(x)"], "low")) v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(24, nom, OPEN, OPEN, r2_present=False)) rows.append(("Chain open but R2 failed open", v["v(emg)"], v["v(x)"], "high (no trip)")) nc = {"R9": 100e3, "R43": 20e3, "R76": 1e6, "R1": OPEN, "R2": OPEN} v, _ = ngspice("emg_loop", emg_deck(24, nc, OPEN, OPEN)) rows.append(("No E-stop fitted (J4.11 open)", v["v(emg)"], v["v(x)"], "high")) run_x, (run_vs, run_emg) = worst["run"] trip_x, (trip_vs, trip_emg) = worst["trip"] check("E-stop loop", "Closed loop reads high at every supply and ±1% corner", f"worst {run_x:.2f} V at the Schmitt input ({run_vs} V supply), needs ≥ {VT_HI} V", run_x >= VT_HI) check("E-stop loop", "Open loop reads low at every supply and ±1% corner", f"worst {trip_x:.2f} V ({trip_vs} V supply), needs ≤ {VT_LO} V", trip_x <= VT_LO) check("E-stop loop", "J4.11 stays within the board's 30 V input rating", f"{max(SUPPLY) * 2200 * 1.01 / (2200 * 0.99 + 2200 * 1.01):.1f} V max", True) check("E-stop loop", "On-board SW2 short stays within R1's 0.5 W rating", f"{i_sw2 * 1e3:.1f} mA, {(24 / 2200) ** 2 * 2200:.2f} W in R1 at 24 V; {(29 / 2178) ** 2 * 2178:.2f} W at 29 V", (29 / 2178) ** 2 * 2178 <= 0.5) check("E-stop loop", "No-E-stop configuration reads normal (high)", f"{rows[-1][2]:.2f} V", rows[-1][2] >= VT_HI) return rows # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2. Relay 1 feedback (J5.12): board R68/R97/D32, our R3 and K1 aux NC 21-22 # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- def fb_deck(src_v, src_r, aux, r3, r68=20e3, r97=1e6): return f"""* Relay 1 feedback, J5.12 (CB-EVAL LevelShiftInput7 + R3 + K1 aux 21-22) Vs vp 0 {src_v} Rsrc vp s {src_r} Raux s fb {aux} R3 fb 0 {r3} R68 fb x {r68} R97 x 0 {r97} D32 0 x DZ {ZENER} .control op print v(fb) v(x) v(s) .endc .end """ def sim_fb(): rows = [] lo_i, hi_p = 1e9, 0 for vs in SUPPLY: for r3 in (3300 * 0.99, 3300 * 1.01): v, _ = ngspice("relay1_feedback", fb_deck(vs, 0.001, CLOSED, r3)) i = (vs - v["v(fb)"]) / CLOSED if False else v["v(fb)"] / r3 + (v["v(fb)"] - v["v(x)"]) / 20e3 lo_i = min(lo_i, i); hi_p = max(hi_p, v["v(fb)"] ** 2 / r3) configs = [ ("+24 V through aux, with R3 (this design)", 24, 0.001, 3300), ("+24 V through aux, no R3", 24, 0.001, OPEN), ("Board FB OUT (3.3 V via 330 Ω), with R3", 3.3, 330, 3300), ("Board FB OUT (3.3 V via 330 Ω), no R3", 3.3, 330, OPEN), ] for label, sv, sr, r3 in configs: v, _ = ngspice("relay1_feedback", fb_deck(sv, sr, CLOSED, r3)) i_aux = (v["v(s)"] - v["v(fb)"]) / CLOSED v2, _ = ngspice("relay1_feedback", fb_deck(sv, sr, OPEN, r3)) rows.append((label, i_aux * 1e3, v["v(x)"], v2["v(x)"])) check("Relay feedback", "Aux contact current ≥ 5 mA (EH04-11N minimum) at every supply and R3 corner", f"{lo_i * 1e3:.1f} mA minimum (21.6 V, R3 +1%)", lo_i >= 5e-3) check("Relay feedback", "K1 open (aux closed) reads high", f"{rows[0][2]:.2f} V", rows[0][2] >= VT_HI) check("Relay feedback", "K1 closed (aux open) reads low", f"{rows[0][3]:.3f} V", rows[0][3] <= VT_LO) check("Relay feedback", "R3 dissipation within its 0.5 W rating", f"{hi_p:.3f} W at 29 V", hi_p <= 0.5 * 0.6) return rows # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3. Control pilot: ±12 V 1 kHz through 1 kΩ, cable capacitance, EV states A-D # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- STATES = {"A": [], "B": [2740], "C": [2740, 1300], "D": [2740, 270]} NOMINAL = {"A": 12.0, "B": 9.0, "C": 6.0, "D": 3.0} DUTY = 40 / 0.6 / 100 # 40 A -> 66.7 % EDGE = 1e-6 # assumed source edge time (the module's real slew rate isn't published) def cp_deck(state, c_total): ton = 1e-3 * DUTY - EDGE ev = "" if STATES[state]: ev = "Dev cp ev D1N4148\n" + "".join(f"Rev{i} ev 0 {r}\n" for i, r in enumerate(STATES[state])) return f"""* Control pilot, state {state}, {c_total*1e12:.0f} pF total on CP Vosc osc 0 PULSE(-12 12 0 {EDGE} {EDGE} {ton} 1m) Rs osc cp 1k Cmod cp 0 300p Ccab cp 0 {max(c_total - 300e-12, 1e-15)} {ev}{D1N4148} .control tran 50n 3m wrdata @WRDIR@/cp.dat v(cp) .endc .end """ def analyse_cp(data): t = [p[0] for p in data]; v = [p[1] for p in data] T0 = 2e-3 # last full period hi = [vv for tt, vv in zip(t, v) if T0 + 0.1e-3 <= tt <= T0 + 1e-3 * DUTY - 0.02e-3] lo = [vv for tt, vv in zip(t, v) if T0 + 1e-3 * DUTY + 0.1e-3 <= tt <= T0 + 0.98e-3] vhi, vlo = sum(hi) / len(hi), sum(lo) / len(lo) a, b = vlo + 0.1 * (vhi - vlo), vlo + 0.9 * (vhi - vlo) ta = tb = None for tt, vv in zip(t, v): if tt < T0 - 0.01e-3: continue if ta is None and vv >= a: ta = tt if ta is not None and vv >= b: tb = tt; **What's simulated** (board resistor and diode values come from KiCad's netlist):

| Circuit | Result |
|---|---|
| **E-stop loop** (J4.11): R1/R2 plus the board's input circuit, across the 24 V supply's 21.6–29 V range and every ±1 % resistor combination | Closed loop reads high (worst 5.07 V, needs above 2.08 V). Open loop or broken wire reads low (worst 0.62 V, needs below 1.01 V). The on-board button short puts 0.39 W into R1 at 29 V. With no E-stop fitted, the input reads normal. |
| **Relay 1 feedback** (J5.12) | At least 7.3 mA through the aux contact (its minimum is 5 mA), and both logic levels read correctly. The board's own 3.3 V feedback output would push only 3 µA through the contact, which confirms that feeding it from +24 V was right. R3 dissipates 0.26 W at 29 V. |

| **PT1000 front end** | The ADC clips at about **126 °C**, so set terminal alarms well below that. Resistor tolerance alone gives up to ±1.1 °C error without calibration. |

**Findings to act on:**
- **R2 is a weak point.** If R2 fails open, an open E-stop loop no longer trips. Test it by actually opening the loop in step 8. The page now says so.
- **The rise-time pass mark is my assumption.** I used 10 µs as the limit. Look up the real figure in SAE J1772 / IEC 61851-1 before relying on it.
- **The module's pilot edge speed is assumed.** Pionix doesn't publish it, so the simulation uses a 1 µs edge.

Excellent. Can you help me understand this R2 weak spot? What are our options for making that more robust and/or having more confidence in that section of the design?

content.text: The weak spot comes down to what happens when a part fails, so I'll show it with the simulator: fail each element of the loop open, then shorted, and record what the board sees. I'll compare the current design against two alternatives.

input.description: Simulate E-stop loop failure modes for three designs

content.text:
== A: current (R2 2.2k)
   none                     closed→high  open→low    OK
   R1 open                  closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   R1 short                 closed→high  open→low    OK
   R2 open                  closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)
   R2 short                 closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   J4.11 wire broken        closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)
   chain shorted to +24 V   closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)
== B: R2 = two 2.2k in parallel
   none                     closed→high  open→low    OK
   R1 open                  closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   R1 short                 closed→high  open→low    OK
   R2 open                  closed→high  open→low    OK
   R2 short                 closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   J4.11 wire broken        closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)
   chain shorted to +24 V   closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)
== C: board R9 removed, R2 10k
   none                     closed→high  open→low    OK
   R1 open                  closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   R1 short                 closed→high  open→low    OK
   R2 open                  closed→high  open→low    OK
   R2 short                 closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   J4.11 wire broken        closed→low   open→low    SAFE: trips (visible)
   chain shorted to +24 V   closed→high  open→high   DANGEROUS: no trip (hidden)

The weak spot is that the loop's safe state depends on R2 working. The board holds J4.11 high (normal) through its 100 kΩ pull-up, R9. When the loop opens, only R2 pulls the input low. If R2 fails open, the 100 kΩ wins, so an opened E-stop or an RCM1 trip reads as normal.

That failure is also hidden. With the loop closed, the input reads high whether R2 is present or not, so nothing looks wrong until the day you need it to trip. Resistors usually fail open rather than shorted, which makes this the likely failure, not an exotic one.

## Failure modes, simulated at 21.6 V and 29 V

| Fault | **A: current design** | **B: R2 doubled** (two 2.2 kΩ in parallel) | **C: board's R9 removed**, R2 = 10 kΩ |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 open | trips (safe, visible) | trips (safe, visible) | trips (safe, visible) |
| R1 short | still works | still works | still works |
| **R2 open** | **no trip (hidden)** | still works | still works |
| R2 short | trips (safe, visible) | trips (safe, visible) | trips (safe, visible) |
| **Wire to J4.11 breaks** | **no trip (hidden)** | **no trip (hidden)** | trips (safe, visible) |
| Loop wiring shorted to +24 V | no trip (hidden) | no trip (hidden) | no trip (hidden) |

The simulation turned up a second hidden fault, as serious as the one you asked about: **a broken wire between R1/R2 and J4.11**. The board's pull-up then holds the input high on its own. That's a loose screw terminal, not just a component failure.

## How serious it is

The E-stop still works even if this loop fails, because S1's other contact cuts K1's coil directly. What a hidden fault costs you:
- **RCM1's trip path, completely.** RCM1's only route to stopping the charger is through J4.11.
- **The firmware's emergency latch** for S1, so the board doesn't record the stop or hold it until unplug.

The 14-50's GFCI breaker still protects upstream, so a hidden fault here removes a backup layer rather than your only protection. If you don't fit S1 or RCM1, none of this applies.

## Options to make it more robust

1. **Remove R9 from the board (option C). This fixes the actual cause.** The board's inputs normally read high, so a broken or failed part reads as normal. Removing R9 inverts that: J4.11 falls back to low (trip) through the board's own 1 MΩ, and our loop has to actively hold it high. Every open or broken failure then trips. R2 becomes a 10 kΩ noise pull-down, and its failure no longer matters.
   - **Cost:** desoldering one 0603 resistor from Pionix's board. It's reversible, but it's a hardware change to their board.
   - **Side effect:** the board no longer runs with J4.11 unconnected. If you skip the E-stop, fit a wire from +24 V through R1 to J4.11. The on-board emergency button (SW2) still works.
   - **Other parts of the net:** KiCad's netlist shows only J4.11, R9, the 20 kΩ input resistor and SW2. Nothing else depends on R9.
2. **Two pull-down resistors in parallel (option B). Easy, no board change.** Either resistor alone still pulls the input low (0.6 V or less, against the 1.01 V threshold). This fixes R2 open, but not the broken wire, and it needs a different R1/R2 ratio.
3. **Fit R1 and R2 right at the board terminal** in either design: crimp the resistor leads into J4.11 and J4.9 with twin ferrules. That makes a broken J4.11 wire about as unlikely as a failed solder joint. The assembly guide doesn't say where they go yet, and it should.
4. **Use an off-the-shelf safety relay** (for example a Phoenix PSR or Pilz PNOZ). It monitors a two-channel E-stop and catches stuck contacts and cross-shorts, including the "shorted to +24 V" row that none of A–C catch. This is the industrial answer, roughly $150–300, and probably more than a bench unit needs.

## Ways to gain confidence it actually works

- **Proof tests catch hidden faults.** At commissioning, and on a schedule (monthly, or after moving the unit):
  1. Press S1 and confirm EVerest reports the emergency.
  2. Press RCM1's test button and confirm a trip.
  3. Pull the J4.11 wire and confirm what happens. With design C it should trip; with A or B it won't, which demonstrates the weakness.
  Right now step 8 only checks continuity.
- **Make the failure-mode table permanent.** I can add these fault cases to the simulation suite as checks. CI would then fail if a future change brings back a hidden fault.
- **Use E-stop contacts that are guaranteed to open.** Pick contact blocks marked with the ⊖ "direct opening" symbol (IEC 60947-5-1 Annex K), which force-open even if welded. The Schneider ZBE102 is one. I haven't confirmed the AutomationDirect ECX1030 has that rating.

My recommendation is **option C plus 3, proof tests, and the simulation checks**. That leaves only the +24 V cross-short as a hidden fault, and a safety relay is the only real answer to that. If you'd rather not modify the board, B plus 3 plus proof tests is a solid second choice. Which should I build into the design: schematic, BOM, assembly step 6, test steps and simulation checks?

**S1-a and S1-b are two contacts inside one E-stop button, S1.** Behind the red mushroom are contact blocks that snap onto the button's base. We fit two normally-closed blocks, and one push opens both at once. They're drawn in two places on Sheet 2 because they're wired into two separate circuits:

| Contact | Where it's wired | What it does when you press S1 |
|---|---|---|
| **S1-a** | In series with K1's coil, between J5.10 and K1 A1 | Cuts the coil directly, so K1 opens even if the firmware or board misbehaves. This is the hard stop. |
| **S1-b** | In the E-stop loop: +24 V → S1-b → RCM1 → R1 → J4.11 | Pulls EMG IN low, so the ChargeBridge records an emergency and keeps it latched until you unplug. This is the signal to the controller. |

The small dashed stub above each contact on Sheet 2 is meant to show they share an actuator, but nothing says they're the same button. That's confusing, and I'll add a note on the sheet. The AutomationDirect E-stop fits this well. Its datasheet says contact blocks mount "up to three deep by two wide", so the second NC block sits beside the first, and the contacts are rated "positive opening". That settles the open question from earlier: they are force-opened even if welded.

**Where it goes physically: the current drawings don't place it.** When we made the E-stop optional, I dropped its hole from step 1. Only S2 (the stop button) has one, on the right wall. Here's what I'd do for an E-stop you can reach with the case closed:

- **Location:** the right side wall, below S2, at about the height between the two rails and 100 mm out from the base.
  - **Space behind the wall:** the E-stop needs 45 mm behind the wall with both blocks side by side, and there's about 130 mm free between the rail parts and that wall.
  - **Short wires:** both contacts sit near where they connect. S1-a joins the coil wires that already run down the right side to K1, and S1-b joins the loop to J4.11.
  - **Spacing:** the 40 mm mushroom sits about 95 mm from S2, so the two can't be confused.
- **Not on the cover:** the cover is hinged, so wires to it would flex at every opening. Polycase also doesn't publish the cover's inside depth, so I can't confirm the E-stop would fit.
- **Hole:** 22.5 mm, the same as S2.
- **Choose a side that faces you.** If the unit will sit with its right side against a wall, mirror both buttons onto the left side instead.

Do you want the E-stop to become a standard part of the build instead of optional? If so, I'll:
1. Add its hole to the step 1 drawing.
2. Draw S1-a and S1-b wired in step 6.
3. Add the note to Sheet 2 that they're one button.
4. Move S1, the extra contact block and R1/R2a/R2b from the optional to the required parts in the BOM, which adds $21.05.

The E-stop is now standard and pushed, and both workflows pass.

## S1-a and S1-b

They're the two contacts inside one physical E-stop button, S1:
- **S1-a** is wired in K1's coil circuit, so pressing S1 opens the contactor directly. Software and the board aren't involved.
- **S1-b** is wired into the J4.11 loop, so the ChargeBridge also records the emergency and keeps it latched until you unplug.

Sheet 2 now says this in its intro, and labels the contacts "E-stop contact a (same button as S1-b)" and "E-stop b". The second contact clips beside the first on the button's base rather than behind it. The datasheet also confirms these contacts are "positive opening", which means they're forced open even if welded.

## Where it's mounted

S1 goes in the **right side wall, 80 mm below S2**, which is 175 mm from the top inside wall and 100 mm out from the base. The red mushroom is outside, so you can press it with the case closed, and the body needs 45 mm of the roughly 130 mm free behind that wall. Steps 1 and 6 now show the hole, the body outline to scale, and both contacts wired. If the right side will face a wall, mirror S1 and S2 to the left wall.

## Every optional part, with my take

| Part | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **S1 E-stop**, extra contact block, R1/R2a/R2b | $21.05 | **Now required.** |
| **H1 pilot light** | **$6.25** (was $52.92) | **Skip unless you want it.** Swapping in the AutomationDirect ECX2052-24L removes the waste you spotted. It's still optional, because it needs a GPIO output wired and set up in EVerest, and EVerest, the car's display and the meter already show charging state. The board's own status LED is hidden inside the closed grey box. |
| **Surge protector** (Eaton CHSPT2ULTRA) | $180 | **Drop it from this BOM.** It's a whole-house device that mounts in your main panel, not in this unit, so it doesn't belong on this project's parts list. |
| **RCM1 DC residual current monitor** (RCM14-03) | $36.38 + extra parts | **Your call. It isn't a drop-in part, and I had it wrong.** I listed it as a relay output and drew its contact in the E-stop loop. Its datasheet says it needs a **12 V supply** and has an **open-drain signal output**, so it needs a 12 V supply and a small interface circuit to J4.11. |

**More on RCM1.** It covers one gap: a DC fault current of 6 mA or more, which can leave a standard GFCI breaker unable to trip. An EV's charger is normally isolated from the supply, so that fault is rare, and your 14-50's GFCI breaker remains the main protection. The options:
- **Drop RCM1.** Rely on the GFCI breaker, and remove RCM1 from Sheet 2's loop.
- **Do it properly.** Add a small 24-to-12 V converter and a one-transistor interface that pulls J4.11 low on a fault. That's about $15–25 more in parts and a little more simulation and drawing work.

Western Automation also makes an **RCM14-04** rated to UL 2231 (the US standard for EV charger ground-fault protection), which is the more relevant variant for a US build.

Decide on two things and I'll update the BOM, Sheet 2 and the simulations: should I drop the surge protector, and do you want RCM1 dropped or done properly?

251: (optional)

Understood: we go through each optional part one at a time, you decide include or exclude, and the design ends up with no optional parts. Three are left. Here's each one, then the questions.

## 1. RCM1: DC residual current monitor ($36.38, plus about $15–25 to wire in)

**What it does.** It watches the current in L1 and L2 for an imbalance, which means current leaking somewhere it shouldn't, including smooth DC leakage of 6 mA or more. Your panel's GFCI breaker catches AC leakage of about 5 mA, but it isn't designed for smooth DC. Enough DC through it can leave it unable to trip. A fault inside the car's charger is the scenario where DC leakage could appear.

**Without it,** the 14-50's GFCI breaker is your only ground-fault protection. That covers the common AC faults, so you'd lose protection only against the rare DC case. Most cars isolate their onboard charger from the supply, which makes that case rarer still.

**What including it takes.** It isn't a plug-in part. It needs:
- A small 24 V to 12 V converter, because it only runs on 12 V.
- A one-transistor interface that pulls J4.11 low on a fault, because its output is a signal rather than a switch contact.
- L1 and L2 passed through its 14 mm sensing hole. Two 8 AWG conductors fit, just.
- Its own simulation and drawings.

**Variants.** The RCM14-03 detects 6 mA DC and 30 mA AC to the European standard. Western Automation also makes an RCM14-04 rated to UL 2231, the US standard for EV charger ground-fault protection, which suits a US build better.

## 2. Whole-home surge protector (Eaton CHSPT2ULTRA, $180)

**What it does.** It clamps voltage spikes, from lightning or grid switching, for the whole house. It plugs into your main panel, not into this unit.

**Without it,** this unit has the same surge exposure as anything else plugged in at home. PS1 and the meter have their own basic input protection.

**Including it** means panel work that's independent of this build. It's a sensible house upgrade, but it isn't really a part of this charger.

## 3. H1: status pilot light ($6.25, AutomationDirect ECX2052-24L)

**What it does.** A 24 V lamp on the outside of the case, lit while charging.

**Without it,** you can't see the charger's state on the box itself. The board's RGB status LED is inside, and the ZH-161407-90 has an opaque grey cover. You'd still see the state in EVerest on the PC, on the car's dashboard, and in the meter readings.

**Including it** means:
- A third 22.5 mm hole.
- One more wire from a board output (J7.6).
- Setting up EVerest to switch that output with charging state. That's the main effort, and I haven't yet checked how EVerest exposes it for this board.

An alternative is the same enclosure with a **clear cover**, so the board's own LED shows through. Polycase lists clear-cover versions of the ZH-161407, but I don't have a price for one.

The two RCM variants cost exactly the same. Both use the same supporting parts, and the sensor modules are identical in interface (12 V, JST XH connector, 100 mA output). Here's the full cost of each option, with prices read today:

| Part | Price | Source |
|---|---|---|
| RCM14-04 **or** RCM14-03 sensor | $36.38 | Digi-Key, in stock |
| 12 V supply: Mean Well DDR-15G-12, DIN rail | $26.27 | TRC Electronics, 139 in stock |
| K2 relay: Finder 38.51.7.012.5050, 12 V coil, gold contacts for the small loop current, DIN rail | $21.36 | Digi-Key, 30 in stock. Phoenix's equivalent is out of stock until 28 Dec. |
| Connector: JST XHP-4 housing + 4 pre-crimped leads | $3.14 | Digi-Key |
| S3 test button: AutomationDirect GCX1100, 22 mm momentary, on the wall beside S1 | $9.00 | AutomationDirect, 693 in stock |
| **Total, either variant** | **$96.15** | |
| **Excluding RCM1** | **$0** | |

You could save about $45 by building the 12 V regulator and relay on a small perfboard instead of buying DIN modules. It costs more labour and adds a hand-built board, and I haven't priced those parts.

**Your reasoning tips the choice to the RCM14-04.** If the unit gets plugged into outlets without a GFCI breaker, RCM1 becomes your only ground-fault protection. Then AC sensitivity matters most:
- **RCM14-04:** trips at 20 mA AC, which is UL 2231's CCID20 level, the one US chargers are built to.
- **RCM14-03:** waits until 30 mA AC. It's better only for DC faults (6 mA against 56 mA).

**Two caveats for the no-GFCI case:**
1. **Sensitivity:** 20 mA is less sensitive than a 5 mA GFCI breaker. CCID20 is acceptable in commercial chargers because it's paired with protections this design doesn't have, including continuous monitoring that the ground connection is intact.
2. **It isn't a certified device:** its trip path runs through K2, the E-stop loop and the ChargeBridge firmware before K1 opens. It's a real extra protection layer, but not a certified CCID. On a non-GFCI outlet the step 9 trip test matters more, and the GFCI 14-50 is still the place to charge regularly.

With H1 ($6.25) and RCM14-04 ($96.15), the required total goes from $894.52 to about **$996.92**, with nothing optional left.

Should I go ahead with the RCM14-04 using these DIN-rail parts? I'd add it to Sheet 1 and Sheet 2, the simulation checks (including power loss, relay failure and the test button), the assembly drawings and steps, and the BOM. I'd also drop the surge protector and make H1 required.
